                           Nutrition and Digestion
Nutrition includes all of those processes by which an animal takes in, digests, absorbs, stores, and uses food
(nutrients) to meet its metabolic needs.

    In this chapter we shall discuss:
    • Animal nutrition,
    • Different strategies animals use for consuming and using food, and
    • Various animal digestive systems.

    Nutrients:
    • A nutrient is a component in foods that an organism uses to survive and grow.
    • Nutrients may be organic or Inorganic.
    • Organic nutrients consist of carbohydrates, fats, proteins (or their building blocks, amino acids), and
       vitamins.
    • Inorganic nutrients: These are dietary minerals, water and oxygen.

Digestion is the chemical and/or mechanical breakdown of complex food into diffusible molecules i.e. particles that
individual cells of an animal can absorb.
    • Starch into glucose.
    • Proteins into amino acids.
    • Fats into fatty acids & glycerol.

Evolution of Nutrition
    •   Green plants and photosynthetic protists have the fewest such nutritional requirements because they can
        synthesize all their own complex molecules from simpler inorganic substances; they are autotrophs.
    •   Animals, fungi, and bacteria that cannot synthesize many of their own organic molecules and must obtain
        them by consuming other organisms or their products are heterotrophs.
    •   Overall, the nutritional requirements of an animal are inversely related to its ability to synthesize molecules
        essential for life.
    •   The fewer such biosynthetic abilities an animal has, the more kinds of nutrients it must obtain from its
        environment.
    •   Animals such as rabbits that survive entirely on plant material are herbivores.
    •   Carnivores such as hawks are animals that eat only meat.
    •   Omnivores such as humans, bears, raccoons, and pigs, eat both plant and animal matter.
    •   Insectivores, such as bats, eat primarily arthropods.

Metabolic Rates of Nutrients in Heterotrophs
The nutrients that a heterotroph ingests can be divided into:
    • Macronutrients and
    • Micronutrients

Macronutrients
  Carbohydrates
  Fats
  Proteins
   • Monosaccharides e.g. Glucose, Fructose, Galactose
   • Disaccharides e.g. Sucrose, Lactose
   • Polysaccharides e.g. Starches, Glycogen

Fats:
    •   Fatty acids
    •   Oils

Micronutrients
   Micronutrients are needed in small quantities and include:
   • Organic vitamins and
   • Inorganic minerals.

Besides these nutrients, animals require water.

Calories and Energy
    •   Calorie: The energy value of food is measured in terms of calories or Calories.
    •   A calorie is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of 1 g of water to 1° C.
    •   A calorie, with a small c, is also called a gram calorie.
    •   A kilocalorie, also known as a Calorie or kilogram calorie (kcal), is equal to 1,000 calories.
    •   Calories in food provide energy in the form of heat so that our bodies can function.
    •   Our bodies’ store and "burn" calories as fuel.
    •   Many dieters count calories and try to decrease caloric intake to lose weight.

 The contractile vacuole is a specialized type of vacuole that regulates the quantity of water inside a cell.
A contractile vacuole is a subcellular structure involved in osmoregulation. The contractile vacuole, as its
name suggests, e xpels water out of the cell by contracting. In freshwater environments, the
concentration of solutes is hypotonic, higher inside than outside the cell. Many freshwater species
(protozoa, sponges), have contractile vacuoles that pump out excess water. Contractile vacuoles are
energy hypoosmotic environments requi ring devices that expel excess water from individual cells
exposed to Some protists and marine invertebrates (e.g., protozoa, cnidarians, echinoderms, sponges)
do not have specialized excretory structures because wastes simply di ffuse into the surrounding
isoosmotic water.

Excretory system in turbellarian ( protonephridia )

A few groups of metazoan invertebrates possess structures, that serve for excretion, osmoregulation, or
both, ther are the nephridia. Among nephridia the sim plest are the protonephridia or flamecell systems.
These are found in flatworms, rotifers, some annelids, and larval molluscs. The protonephridial
excretory system is composed of a network of excretory canals that open to the outside of the body

Intracellular and Extracellular

Intracellular:

 In intracellular digestion breakdown of food occurs within the cells. First food in taken into the cell

Extra cellular

In extra cellular digestion, the enzymes are secreted outside the cell into the gut cavity or lumen where
digestion occurs.

Nutrients from the food then pass into body cells for energy metabolism or biosynthesis.

Question: 1
Discuss the digestive system in different invertebrates?

Solution:
Introduction:
Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.

Their digestive systems vary depending on their structure and way of life.

Some have no digestive organs, while others have well-developed systems.

Digestion can be inside cells (intracellular) or in a body cavity (extracellular).

1.Porifera (Sponges)
Type: No true digestive system

System: Simple; no mouth or stomach

Process: Water flows through pores; special cells (choanocytes) trap and digest food inside the cells
(intracellular digestion).

2.Cnidaria (Hydra, Jellyfish)
Type: Incomplete digestive system (one opening)

System: Gastrovascular cavity

Process: Food enters and exits through the same opening. It is digested in the cavity (extracellular), and
nutrients are absorbed by body cells.

3.Platyhelminthes (Flatworms)
Type: Incomplete digestive system

System: Branched gut with one opening

Process: Food enters and exits from one opening. Some parasitic species absorb nutrients directly from
the host, as they lack a digestive system.

4.Nematoda (Roundworms)
Type: Complete digestive system

System: Tube-like structure with mouth and anus

Process: Food enters through the mouth, is digested in the gut, nutrients are absorbed, and waste exits
through the anus.

5.Annelida (Earthworms)
Type: Complete and organized digestive system

System: Mouth → Pharynx → Esophagus → Crop → Gizzard → Intestine → Anus

Process: Food is swallowed, stored, ground, digested, and absorbed in order. Waste is passed out from
the anus.

6.Arthropoda (Insects, Crabs, Spiders)
Type: Complete and specialized system

Systems: Foregut, Midgut, Hindgut

Process: Food is chewed, partially digested in the foregut, digested and absorbed in the midgut, and
waste is removed through the hindgut.

7.Mollusca (Snails, Octopus, Clams)
Type: Complete digestive system

System: Includes mouth, stomach, intestine, and digestive glands

Process: A radula scrapes food (in some), digestion occurs in the stomach and intestine, and nutrients
are absorbed.

8.Echinodermata (Starfish, Sea Urchins)
Type: Complete but unique system

System: Mouth, stomach (extendable in starfish), intestine, anus

Process: Starfish push their stomachs out to digest food outside their bodies; sea urchins chew food with
Aristotle’s lantern.

Conclusion:
Invertebrate digestive systems range from very simple (like sponges) to advanced (like arthropods).

Some use cells for digestion, while others have complete systems with separate mouth and anus.

Each type of digestive system fits the animal’s feeding method and environment.

This variety shows how invertebrates adapt to survive in different habitats.

Describe how energy is generated from different nutrients in heterotrophic
Organisms?

Heterotrophic organisms obtain energy by oxidizing organic nutrients—primarily carbohydrates,
lipids and proteins—via a series of interconnected pathways. The overall goal is to harvest the
chemical energy in nutrient bonds and convert it into ATP, the cell’s energy “currency.” Below
is an overview of how each major class of nutrient is catabolized for ATP production.

1. Carbohydrate Catabolism

   1. Glycolysis (in the cytosol)
         o Substrate: Glucose (6-carbon)
         o Process: A ten-step pathway that splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate
             (3-carbon), generating:
                 ▪ 2 ATP (net) by substrate-level phosphorylation
                 ▪ 2 NADH (each carrying high-energy electrons)
         o Fate of products:
                 ▪ Pyruvate is transported into mitochondria (in eukaryotes) for further
                     oxidation.
                 ▪ NADH enters the electron transport chain to drive additional ATP
                     synthesis.
   2. Pyruvate Oxidation
         o Location: Mitochondrial matrix
         o Process: Each pyruvate is decarboxylated and linked to coenzyme A, forming
             acetyl-CoA, while producing one NADH per pyruvate.
   3. Citric Acid (TCA) Cycle
         o Location: Mitochondrial matrix
         o Process: Acetyl-CoA (2-carbon) condenses with oxaloacetate (4-carbon) to cycle
             through reactions that:
                 ▪ Release 2 CO₂
                 ▪ Produce 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, and 1 GTP (or ATP) per acetyl-CoA
         o Yield per glucose: since one glucose → 2 acetyl-CoA, the TCA cycle yields 6
             NADH, 2 FADH₂, and 2 GTP.
   4. Oxidative Phosphorylation
         o Location: Inner mitochondrial membrane
         o Process: NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the electron transport chain,
             creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase:
                 ▪ ~2.5 ATP per NADH
                 ▪ ~1.5 ATP per FADH₂
         o Total yield: Complete oxidation of one glucose yields approximately 30–32 ATP.
